question: SQ-LIP-000009
text: Is lipedema linked to gluten sensitivity, celiac disease, or HLA-DQ2/DQ8?
minor_problems: [minor] set: E3 and E4 are two papers on the same NHANES sample (n=3833, same 11 celiac cases) used for P2 and P3; they should be read as one dataset, not independent confirmations.

[minor] set: No proposition addresses gluten sensitivity or celiac disease prevalence in lipedema directly; the only direct evidence is HLA typing (E1), so the question's celiac/gluten parts remain unanswered.

[minor] P1: stance errors ['E6'] — suggested: Limited evidence suggests celiac-associated HLA-DQ risk haplotypes are somewhat more frequent in women with lipedema than in the general population. (E1 carries the claim. E6 is one typed patient, not a frequency (and the authors cite E1 figures), so it should be context. 'Small effect size' rests on a contingency coefficient; relative differences for DQ8 and both haplotypes are not small. E2 has an empty quote.)

[minor] P3: not fully supported; overgeneralized — suggested: Limited, underpowered evidence suggests a lipedema-like fat phenotype may not differ in prevalence between women with and without celiac disease autoimmunity. (Null result from 1 of 11 celiac cases; the phenotype is a proxy from body composition. A non-difference at this power is weak.)

[minor] P4: not fully supported; overgeneralized — suggested: Food-specific IgG reactivity to barley may be similar in women with and without lipedema, although total IgG appears lower in lipedema. (Only barley (93.8 vs 93.2%) is shown; 'gluten-containing cereals' (wheat, rye) is not in the item. Near-universal positivity makes the comparison uninformative.)

propositions.statement: Celiac-associated HLA-DQ risk haplotypes are reported more frequently in women with lipedema than in the general population, with a small effect size.
propositions.rationale: One cross-sectional sample compared against a historical population comparator found higher HLA-DQ2/DQ8 carriage, with a near-zero contingency coefficient; a male case adds an isolated observation.

evidence.finding: In 95 women with lipedema, HLA-DQ2 47.4% vs 41.2%, HLA-DQ8 22.1% vs 11.3%, any HLA 61.1% vs 53.7%, both 7.4% vs 1.2% versus a Brazilian population comparator (p<0.0001), but contingency coefficient near zero.
Provides the general-population HLA-DQ2/DQ8 prevalence data (Brazilian population, celiac patients and relatives) used as the historical comparator for the lipedema HLA comparison.
In a case series of five men with lipedema, the only patient who underwent HLA typing was positive for both HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8; a gluten-free diet was applied based on this positivity.

propositions.statement: Women with serologically confirmed celiac disease may have lower gynoid and leg fat than women without celiac disease, including among those with overweight or obesity.
propositions.rationale: A population sample found an inverse association between celiac autoimmunity and the gynoid fat distribution typical of lipedema, based on very few celiac cases.

evidence.finding: In NHANES (n=3833, only 11 celiac cases), celiac women had lower gynoid fat (39.5% vs 42.6%, p=0.0007), 20.3% less leg fat and lower leg/trunk ratio; reduction persisted among overweight/obese women (-8.7%, p=0.005).

propositions.statement: The prevalence of a lipedema-like fat phenotype does not appear to differ between women with and without celiac disease autoimmunity.
propositions.rationale: In the same population sample the lipedema phenotype was not more or less frequent among celiac women and showed no dose-response pattern.

evidence.finding: Lipedema phenotype in 1/11 celiac (9.1%) vs 282/3822 non-celiac women (7.4%), p=0.570; no dose-response across leg/trunk ratio quartiles (p for trend 0.893; rho=-0.002).

propositions.statement: Food-specific IgG reactivity to gluten-containing cereals appears similar in women with lipedema and in comparison women.
propositions.rationale: Food-specific IgG testing showed near-identical barley reactivity, alongside fewer total IgG and a non-significantly higher count of positive reactions in lipedema.

evidence.finding: In 234 women, barley IgG positivity was 93.8% in lipedema vs 93.2% in comparators; positive food reactions were slightly but not significantly more numerous (p=0.186) while total IgG was markedly lower (1747 vs 2975 AU; p<0.001).

propositions.statement: The main celiac-associated HLA-DQ haplotype is the principal genetic risk determinant for celiac disease, through presentation of gliadin peptides to helper T cells.
propositions.rationale: Background on the celiac side of the hypothesis; it does not address lipedema directly.

evidence.finding: Review describes HLA-DQ2 as the main genetic risk determinant for celiac disease, with DQ2 presentation of gliadin to CD4+ T cells central to its pathogenesis; lipedema is not discussed.
